title: Instance Metadata Service Version 2
summary: Instance metadata service version 2 is the session-oriented revision of the link-local endpoint that cloud instances query to obtain information about themselves, most importantly the temporary credentials associated with their attached role. The original interface answered any request arriving from the instance, which meant that a server-side request forgery flaw in an application running on that instance was sufficient to read the instance role credentials and use them from anywhere on the internet. Version two changes the exchange in two ways: the client must first issue a PUT request to obtain a limited-lifetime token that is unique to that session, and every subsequent metadata request must present that token in a header, with a configurable hop limit that additionally restricts whether requests can traverse a proxy or container network layer. Because a naive request-forgery payload cannot set custom headers or perform the required PUT, the token requirement breaks the common exploit chain, while the hop limit constrains forwarding through intermediate proxies and container namespaces. Security teams track adoption by measuring how many instances still permit the older interface, since the setting is enforced per instance and inherited at launch, and they apply it to container platforms through the node launch configuration. The topic also covers the practical migration problems: software that read metadata directly, custom agents that proxy metadata to pods, and the need to monitor metadata requests as a detection signal.
objectives: You will be able to explain how the token and hop limit requirements break credential theft through a server-side request forgery flaw.
You will be able to determine whether an instance or node pool still permits the legacy unauthenticated metadata interface.
You will be able to migrate applications and agents that read metadata directly without breaking startup.
You will be able to configure hop limits appropriately for proxies, containers and load balancers.
You will be able to use metadata access patterns as a detection signal for in-instance compromise.
